problem: Prior VLN work runs on a discrete navigation graph (R2R) or with discrete, deterministic actions (VLN-CE). Both assume known topology, perfect localization and obstacle-free motion between viewpoints, so they do not test real robot control. Flat seq2seq and cross-modal-attention VLN agents built for short-horizon nav-graph settings transfer poorly to long-horizon continuous control.
motivation: Real robots must output continuous velocities over very long horizons and must avoid obstacles. Robo-VLN episodes average 326 steps, versus 55.8 in VLN-CE and 5 in R2R. The authors observe that a single flat policy must handle both cross-modal instruction grounding and low-level control. Because of this, it fails on long trajectories and repeatedly bumps into obstacles, which suggests separating reasoning from imitation of a controller.
key_idea: Split continuous VLN into two levels. A high-level policy uses language–vision cross-attention to predict a discrete sub-goal (forward 0.25 m / turn 15° / stop). A low-level imitation policy converts that sub-goal and the visual features into continuous linear and angular velocities.
insight: The gain comes from the hierarchical structure, not from extra supervision. In the ablation (Table III), a flattened model given the same sub-goal auxiliary supervision reaches 40 SR / 34 SPL on val-unseen, while the hierarchical model reaches 46 / 40. Aligning RGB and depth separately with the instruction works much better than early RGB-D fusion (34 vs 46 SR on unseen). Removing vision drops the agent to random level (7 SR). Among the flat baselines, plain Seq2Seq (33 SR unseen) beats PM and CMA (28 SR), which suggests that discrete-VLN attention tricks do not transfer to long-horizon continuous control.
method: Robo-VLN dataset construction: an A* planner gives high-level oracle actions. A feedback controller turns the R2R sparse waypoints into continuous (v, ω) commands for a differential-drive Locobot mesh, and Locobot dynamics roll the state forward. Collision checking removes non-navigable paths such as stairs, keeping 71% of VLN-CE trajectories (3177 trajectories, 9533 instruction-trajectory pairs).

Multi-modal cross-attention encoder: BERT word embeddings plus sinusoidal positional encoding serve as queries. Two separate (non-shared) Transformer blocks (hidden 256, 4 heads, FF 1024) cross-attend over 7x7x2048 spatial features, one from ImageNet ResNet-50 on RGB and one from a DD-PPO-pretrained ConvNet on depth.

High-level attention decoder: an LSTM takes the RGB-attended and depth-attended contexts, the mean-pooled visual features and the previous action. A softmax head outputs a sub-goal in {forward 0.25 m, turn-left 15°, turn-right 15°, stop}.

Low-level imitation policy: stacked LSTMs take the mean-pooled visual features and the high-level sub-goal, with no language input. One-layer MLP heads output tanh-bounded linear and angular velocity and a sigmoid stop probability, conditioned on the previous low-level action.

Training: a joint loss weights cross-entropy on high-level actions by λ and weights (MSE on velocities + BCE on stop) by (1−λ). Supervision is teacher-forced imitation of the oracle controller, with truncated BPTT (length 100), 20 epochs, and early stopping on val-seen.
Episode definition: success means the agent ends within 3 m of the goal and stops, either via the stop action or with angular velocity below a threshold. The episode cap is 1000 steps.

setting.backbone: ImageNet ResNet-50 (RGB) + DD-PPO-pretrained ConvNet (depth) + BERT word embeddings + Transformer cross-attention + LSTM high/low-level policies (trained with imitation learning)
setting.training_data: Robo-VLN train split: R2R human instructions ported to continuous Locobot trajectories in Matterport3D (3177 trajectories / 9533 instruction-trajectory pairs across all splits). Oracle A* high-level actions and feedback-controller velocity labels. No DAgger, no speaker augmentation.
setting.action_space: continuous linear & angular velocity (v, ω) + discrete stop. Internal high-level sub-goal is FORWARD 0.25 m / TURN 15° / STOP.
setting.simulator: Habitat (Matterport3D reconstructions, Locobot mesh with dynamics model)

numbers_note: Only validation splits are reported; there are no test-server results. Robo-VLN is the paper's own benchmark (a 71% subset of VLN-CE R2R trajectories ported to continuous velocity control), so its numbers are not comparable to R2R-CE. The no-vision ablation (#1) is omitted here; its val-unseen TL/NE columns appear swapped in the table (TL 10.2, NE 4.81). Metrics are printed as fractions (e.g. 0.46) and converted to 0-100.
results: On Robo-VLN val-unseen, HCM reaches 46 SR / 40 SPL / 0.35 nDTW / 7.94 NE. The best flat baseline, Seq2Seq, reaches 33 SR / 30 SPL, so HCM is about 13 points better in SR and 10 in SPL. PM and CMA baselines do worse still (28 SR). Val-seen results follow the same pattern (49 SR vs 36 for Seq2Seq). Qualitatively, the flat agent collides with obstacles, while HCM completes episodes of more than 500 steps.
limitations: Simulation only, with no real-robot deployment, even though the paper is framed around robotics. Evaluation covers val-seen and val-unseen only, with no held-out test split.

Baselines are VLN-CE reimplementations without DAgger or data augmentation. HCM itself is trained purely by teacher-forced imitation, so exposure bias remains and the comparison against stronger flat agents is not tested.

The intro claims modularized, separate training, but both policies are in fact trained jointly with a weighted loss. The low-level policy does not see language, and the benchmark drops 29% of trajectories (stairs, obstacles), which limits comparability with VLN-CE.
